title: Temporal slab hierarchy and thin-checkpoint reclaimer for low-latency KV reuse
author: Marisol Ortega
description:
Context and motivation:
This PR introduces a temporal slab hierarchy plus a lightweight 'thin-checkpoint' reclaimer to improve block reuse latency in the paged KV cache. Workloads with many short lived keys and bursty request patterns were suffering from allocation churn and pin-contention at the 95/99 tail. Instead of a single monolithic slab we organize blocks into a small number of time-segmented slabs (hot, warm, cold) and add a thin checkpoint that records compacted allocation metadata for fast reclaim without a full sweep.

Design summary:
- Temporal slab hierarchy: newly-allocated blocks are placed into the hot slab. A background epoch tick (configurable, default 30s) moves stabilized blocks to warm and eventually cold slabs. The movement is metadata-only (pointer and epoch stamp) to avoid data migrations. Slab boundaries are tunable per-instance and exposed via runtime config.
- Thin-checkpoint reclaimer: periodic lightweight checkpoints capture block occupancy bitmaps and small freelist deltas. Checkpoints are small (typically <4KB) and used to accelerate reclaim decisions in the common case; we fall back to the full reclaim path for noisy epochs.
- Fast reuse path: when an allocation request can accept relaxed contiguity, the allocator consults the checkpoint to satisfy requests from recently freed blocks in hot/warm slabs without taking heavy locks. This minimizes blocking on the global freelist.
- Deferred soft-eviction: instead of immediate hard eviction during pin contention, we introduce a soft-evict hint which defers scoring for a short window to allow in-flight allocations to finish, reducing thrash under bursty traffic.

Checklist (implementation):
- [x] Temporal slab metadata and epoch tick loop
- [x] Thin checkpoint generator and on-disk serialization for optional debugging
- [x] Fast reuse allocator path with optimistic lockless check and fallback
- [x] Soft-evict hinting and scoring window
- [x] Configuration knobs exposed in allocator::Config + console telemetry
- [x] Unit tests for slab transitions and checkpoint validity
- [x] Microbench harness for allocation/reclaim latency

Performance summary (microbench on p4-standard with typical small-token generator workload):
- 99th percentile allocation latency reduced from 1.6ms -> 1.38ms (~14% reduction)
- Median allocation latency reduced from 0.28ms -> 0.24ms (~14% reduction)
- Sustained throughput for small-token requests increased by ~18% in contention scenarios due to reduced lock stalls
- Effective cache hit rate improved by ~9% for workloads with frequent short-lived keys because reuse is faster and softer eviction reduces premature reclamation

Compatibility and safety:
- The thin checkpoint format is versioned. On startup the allocator falls back to the old reclaim path if encountering an unknown checkpoint version.
- Default configuration keeps prior behavior (checkpointing disabled) unless the feature flag allocator.temporal_slab=true is enabled. We rolled this behind a console toggle to allow staged rollouts.

Testing and validation:
- Unit and integration tests included for: slab state transitions, optimistic fast-path correctness, checkpoint serialization roundtrip, and soft-evict scoring heuristics.
- Added a microbench harness (bench/alloc_reclaim) used to produce the numbers above; harness included in CI as a non-blocking job.
- Dogfood run: deployed to perf-canary for 48h on a subset of traffic; telemetry shows expected tail improvements and no increase in OOM or error rates.

Related work and follow-ups:
- ENG-4289: allocator refactor to split slab metadata (this PR builds on that refactor)
- ENG-4317: console runtime knobs and telemetry work for allocation metrics (explicit telemetry counters added here)
- Follow-up tasks: integrate thin-checkpoint with cross-shard reuse and evaluate adaptive epoch tuning based on observed request patterns.

Review thread (high level):
- Asha: requested stronger invariants around epoch ordering and suggested making the epoch tick jittered to avoid global sync storms; asked for an assert in debug build to validate checkpoint monotonicity.
- Marisol (author): addressed comment by adding jitter and debug-only monotonicity checks; pushed fixup commit.
- Liam: raised concern about checkpoint size on high cardinality workloads; requested a cap and eviction rule.
- Marisol: added a configurable checkpoint cap and a sampling-based sketch to keep checkpoints bounded; documented tradeoffs.
- Ravi: did a safety pass on fallback correctness; approved after small test additions.

Review comments (representative snippets):
- "Asha Patel: The epoch tick should be jittered, otherwise instances will align and cause short bursts of GC-like activity. Add a per-instance jitter and document the default."
- "Liam McCoy: We need to protect against unbounded checkpoint growth when there are many tiny keys. Can we cap and evict least-recently-updated entries from the checkpoint?"
- "Ravi Singh: Fast-path looks good but ensure we never hand out a block that is concurrently being reclaimed; the fallback must be rock solid."

Merge and rollout:
- Merge method: squash
- Merged at: 2024-05-22
- Post-merge: feature flag allocator.temporal_slab=false by default; staged rollout performed via console to 5% -> 25% -> 100% over two weeks after merge. Observability dashboards added to the allocator overview in console.

Release notes:
- Introduced temporal slab hierarchy and a thin-checkpoint reclaimer to reduce allocation latency and improve reuse under bursty workloads. Feature is off by default and gated behind allocator.temporal_slab. Expect reduced allocation tail latency and higher throughput for small-token workloads when enabled.

Notes for on-call and incident responders:
- If errors related to checkpoint parsing appear, disable allocator.temporal_slab (console toggle) to revert to legacy reclaim.
- Checkpoint files (when enabled) are stored under /var/lib/redwood/allocator/checkpoints (debug-only and optional); do not rely on them for correctness in short-term recovery.
